title: Intensity and amplitude
prior_knowledge_summary: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle or point on a wave from its equilibrium position.
A progressive wave transfers energy without a net transfer of matter.
From Lesson 7, intensity is power transferred per unit area normal to the energy transfer, and I=P/A.
new_learning: Use intensity proportional to amplitude squared for a progressive wave.
Compare amplitudes using intensity ratios and interpret intensity-amplitude graphs.
not_yet_taught: Explain the Doppler effect for a moving sound source.
Combine waves by superposition or calculate interference intensity.

blocks.heading: Twice the movement, twice the intensity?
content: Two otherwise identical progressive waves pass identical detectors. The particles in one wave have twice the amplitude. A first guess is that its intensity is twice as large. The detector says four times as large. Why?
Amplitude measures displacement, but wave energy depends more strongly on the size of that oscillation. We need a squared relationship.

figure.purpose: Create the need for the square relationship.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sketch of two otherwise identical sinusoidal waves with amplitudes A and 2A entering identical detectors. Show detector readings I and 4I only after the visual comparison, with no derivation.
figure.alt_text: A wave with twice the amplitude gives four times the intensity.

blocks.heading: The formula to remember
content: The formula to remember is $I \propto A^2$. Here $I$ is intensity in W m$^{-2}$ and $A$ is amplitude in metres, m.
For two otherwise comparable progressive waves, $\frac{I_2}{I_1}=\left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right)^2$. This ratio form removes the unknown constant of proportionality.
The controlled definition is: amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle or point on a wave from its equilibrium position.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the maximum displacement of a particle or point on a wave from its equilibrium position

figure.purpose: Connect amplitude measurement to the square law and ratio form.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful sketch with equilibrium line, amplitude arrow from equilibrium to crest, then a clean flow I proportional to A squared and I2/I1=(A2/A1) squared. Keep labels sparse.
figure.alt_text: Amplitude is measured from equilibrium to a crest, and intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.

blocks.heading: From amplitude change to intensity change
content: A progressive wave changes from amplitude 3.0 mm to 4.5 mm. The amplitude ratio is $4.5/3.0=1.5$.
$I_2/I_1=(1.5)^2=2.25$. The new intensity is 2.25 times the original intensity.
Check the direction: the amplitude increased, so the intensity ratio must be greater than one. Squaring 1.5 should also give a value greater than 1.5.

figure.purpose: Model a complete amplitude-to-intensity ratio calculation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout showing A1=3.0 mm, A2=4.5 mm, amplitude ratio 1.5, square step, intensity ratio 2.25, and a direction check. Do not convert millimetres because equal units cancel.
figure.alt_text: Increasing amplitude from 3.0 to 4.5 millimetres increases intensity by a factor of 2.25.

blocks.heading: Working backward needs a square root
content: If intensity changes are known, reverse the square relationship: $A_2/A_1=\sqrt{I_2/I_1}$.
Suppose intensity falls to 36% of its original value. The amplitude ratio is $\sqrt{0.36}=0.60$, so amplitude falls to 60% of its original value.
This is different from a direct proportion. A 64% fall in intensity corresponds to a 40% fall in amplitude.

figure.purpose: Teach reverse solving and distinguish percentage changes.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison panel. Show intensity ratio 0.36 entering a square-root step and amplitude ratio 0.60 emerging. Contrast 36 percent remains with 60 percent amplitude remains.
figure.alt_text: An intensity ratio of 0.36 gives an amplitude ratio of 0.60.

blocks.heading: Linking Lesson 7 to amplitude
content: At detector 1, a wave has intensity 72 W m$^{-2}$. At detector 2, the same kind of wave transfers 9.0 W through a normal area of 0.50 m$^2$.
Now use the square root: $A_2/A_1=\sqrt{0.25}=0.50$. The amplitude at detector 2 is half that at detector 1.
An independent check squares 0.50 to recover the intensity ratio 0.25.

figure.purpose: Show a safe two-stage link from power and area to amplitude ratio.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-stage worked flow. Stage 1: P and A give I2. Carry I2=18 W m minus two with unit. Stage 2: compare with I1=72 W m minus two and square-root to get amplitude ratio 0.50. Include a square-back check.
figure.alt_text: Power and area give intensity, then an intensity ratio gives an amplitude ratio.

blocks.heading: Why the graph is a curve
content: It feels natural to draw a straight line for intensity against amplitude because both quantities increase together. The mistake is treating proportional to $A^2$ as proportional to $A$.
An $I$ against $A$ graph passes through the origin and curves upward. Doubling $A$ makes $I$ four times larger, and tripling $A$ makes $I$ nine times larger.
A graph of $I$ against $A^2$ is instead a straight line through the origin. Always read the horizontal axis before choosing the shape.

figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper side-by-side axes. Left: I against A upward curve through origin with points (1,1), (2,4), (3,9). Right: I against A squared straight line through origin. No numerical scale or gradient calculation.
figure.alt_text: Intensity against amplitude curves upward, while intensity against amplitude squared is a straight line.

blocks.heading: Choose the direction of the ratio
content: For amplitude to intensity, form $A_2/A_1$ and square it. For intensity to amplitude, form $I_2/I_1$ and take its square root.
Keep numerator labels consistent. If the question asks for the new value compared with the original, every ratio should be new divided by original.
Check the direction, the scale and the graph shape. A larger amplitude must give a larger intensity, but the intensity changes by the square of the amplitude factor.

figure.purpose: Provide a compact decision routine without giving practice answers.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper decision map: amplitude ratio known leads to square; intensity ratio known leads to square root; graph requested leads to read axes. Add checks for consistent labels and change direction.
figure.alt_text: A decision map chooses squaring, square rooting, or graph interpretation.

visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

misconceptions_addressed: Intensity is directly proportional to amplitude.
An intensity ratio can be used directly as an amplitude ratio.
Every intensity-amplitude graph is a straight line.
next_lesson_can_assume: Use I proportional to A squared.
Find amplitude ratios from intensity ratios.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Explain Doppler shift from wavefront spacing.
